transcript:
Meeting: Redwood edgecases demo -- long context / high TPS / streaming/backpressure/timeouts
Date/Time: 2026-05-06 15:30 UTC
Duration: 43 minutes
Attendees: Alice Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Reyes (Redwood SE), Jared Kim (Nimbus CTO), Sana Patel (Nimbus SRE), Miguel Alvarez (Nimbus ML)

[00:00] Alice Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, i'm alice from redwood, i'll hand it over to marco for the deep parts but quick agenda: we'll cover API demo for long-context, how console and optimize surfaces recommendations, then go into streaming backpressure and timeout behaviors and POC next steps
[00:12] Jared Kim: sounds good, we only have 45 so appreciate being concise
[00:18] Marco Reyes: cool, quick context - you told us you have use cases with >50k token contexts and bursts at 400-600 TPS, is that still accurate? just to confirm
[00:34] Miguel Alvarez: yeah, roughly, we run reconciliation jobs that attach months of transaction history, and chat assistants that keep long sessions. bursts are the main worry, and timeouts at the LB layer right now kill streams
[00:50] Marco Reyes: okay, perfect. so first, long context - redwood supports up to 100k-ish context depending on model/quantization, but there are trade offs. we use selective kv prefix caching and chunked attention to avoid reprocessing entire context for each token. in practice you want to pin recurring prefixes - e.g., customer profile - into the KV cache so subsequent requests are smaller
[01:20] Sana Patel: when you say kv cache, do you mean the key-value cache on the gpu? we saw docs that reference kv cash... sorry kv cash in notes lol
[01:31] Marco Reyes: yep, kv cache - and the auto-prefix cache can be persisted per-session on dedicated pools. note: on hosted api we keep short-lived caches by default for security reasons, but we have options for longer caches in dedicated/private
[01:52] Jared Kim: how does that interact with versioned models? if we roll models fast, will the cache be invalidated often
[02:05] Marco Reyes: good q - cache is tied to model family/format. if you change tokenizers or architecture, cache is invalidated. for minor version bumps we support warm migrations where the runtime can fallback to compatible kernels - there's a small compatibility table
[02:28] Alice Chen: demo time - i'll show the console view while marco runs a high-tps replay
[02:35] Marco Reyes: starting replay now. so we have a scripted load generator hitting the hosted endpoint at 500 rps with a mix of long-context and short-context traffic; i'm going to enable streaming with chunk size 128 tokens and a client-side 10s per-chunk timeout
[03:00] [03:00] Marco Reyes: (system) replayer: started 500 rps
[03:12] Miguel Alvarez: wait are you doing combined streaming and long-context? won't that blow up latency
[03:20] Marco Reyes: it's the worst case scenario - that's why we built the demo. watch the traces, i'll open the per-token latency panel in the console
[03:35] [03:35] Marco Reyes: okay, first interesting thing: we see a subset of requests hitting a backpressure signal on the serving layer - requests that exceed the per-GPU queueing threshold are held and either batched into the next kernel window or, if TTL expires, we materialize a timeout path
[04:00] Sana Patel: what's the timeout path? do you return partial streaming chunks or an error? we need predictable behaviour for our app
[04:12] Marco Reyes: by default we return a clear status code and an error event on the stream, plus the last fully emitted chunk. you can opt into graceful-degradation where we trim context (drop nonessential prefixes) and synthesize a short answer; that's handy for chat with fairness requirements
[04:38] Jared Kim: trimming context sounds risky - could that change the answer in unacceptable ways
[04:45] Marco Reyes: yes - it's a quality tradeoff. Optimize (the product) can run evals on your prompt-set to tell you which prefixes are low-impact and safe to drop. you can also configure fallback models - e.g., fallback to a smaller, faster variant that preserves essential semantics but has less compute
[05:12] Miguel Alvarez: can you talk about backpressure specifics? our infra uses nginx LB with 30s keepalives and then cuts
[05:22] Marco Reyes: so two places for timeouts: client LB and our gateway. we recommend using streaming keepalives and configuring the LB to allow longer per-request windows when using streaming. for hosted we have a default gateway timeout of 60s per-total-request, but for dedicated we can tune that. also we support chunk-level heartbeats so the LB sees activity
[05:48] Sana Patel: chunk-level heartbeats, is that the SSE ping? how heavy is it
[05:55] Marco Reyes: it's a tiny keepalive event every 2-3s, negligible bandwidth. it's emitted when there's any stall between chunks to prevent LB timeouts
[06:10] Alice Chen: note that client-side retries should be idempotent-safe. for streaming we suggest an at-most-once approach for partial outputs, or re-run the whole request if you can dedupe downstream. we'll include example code in the runbook
[06:28] Jared Kim: ok, show us metrics - where do we look in the console
[06:35] Marco Reyes: panel is open - per-route token latency, queue depth, requeue events, and a small histogram of tail latency. also you'll see an 'eviction' metric when the KV cache drops prefixes under memory pressure
[06:54] [06:54] Marco Reyes: i'm toggling the requeue policy to 'aggressive batching' to see the effect - this will batch more requests into kernel windows but increase tail latency slightly, which may be acceptable if you value throughput
[07:18] Miguel Alvarez: that's interesting; what's the batching window size range
[07:24] Marco Reyes: 5-30ms typically, adjustable. at high TPS we widen window to get better kernel utilization. Optimize recommends a config based on your latency SLO and token size distribution
[07:40] Sana Patel: at 500 RPS we care about SLO 200ms p95, can you hit that with long contexts
[07:49] Marco Reyes: p95 200ms with long-context mixed workload is tough on hosted. with dedicated + caching + aggressive batching, yes - also quantization helps a lot, the runtime picks int8 kernels where applicable to reduce per-token compute
[08:10] Alice Chen: just to call out - we often recommend a hybrid: hosted for non-sensitive or lower-cost routes and dedicated pools for the latency-sensitive, long-context heavy flows
[08:26] Jared Kim: curious about costs - how much more would dedicated be versus hosted for sustained 500 RPS peaks
[08:35] Alice Chen: cost depends on commit level. Roughly, think of a dedicated pool as paying for the compute reservation but you'll see lower per-token unit cost and fewer failures. we'll send a modelled cost scenario in the spreadsheet
[08:50] Miguel Alvarez: can you show an intentional timeout so we can see the streaming behaviour end-to-end
[08:56] Marco Reyes: sure, i'm going to shrink the per-GPU queue so we trigger backpressure - now
[09:05] [09:05] Marco Reyes: (system) triggered queue eject on GPU-3
[09:12] Sana Patel: ok we got a bunch of 'stream error' events - i see partial chunks and an 'error: request_timeout' in logs
[09:24] Marco Reyes: yep that's the default; note the last chunk is still returned. if you prefer we can return a structured fallback response like 'truncated=true' with a short summary generated from the trimmed context
[09:42] Jared Kim: for compliance we need audit logs showing which model served the request and which fallback was used - do you surface that
[09:50] Marco Reyes: yes, console logs include model_id, variant, kernel profile id, and policy flags like 'truncated=true' and 'fallback_variant'. we can also stream these events to your SIEM via log-forwarding
[10:08] Alice Chen: quick interruption - customer asked about SSO and SOC2 earlier, we have the security pack link in chat
[10:15] Miguel Alvarez: saw it, thanks
[10:18] Marco Reyes: back to performance - another mitigation is adaptive routing: route latency-critical requests to reserved dedicated nodes in a separate pool, and best-effort requests to shared capacity
[10:33] Sana Patel: how fast can you spin up capacity if we get a sudden increase? autoscaling is okay but cold start for GPUs is heavy
[10:42] Marco Reyes: autoscaling for dedicated uses a warm-standby model; we keep a hot buffer and can burst within seconds to a couple of minutes depending on request patterns. for hosted we have more elastic supply but it's multi-tenant so you may hit noisy neighbor at extremes
[11:05] Jared Kim: can we get a custom SLA around these bursts
[11:11] Alice Chen: yes that's part of the dedicated contract; we'll propose latency and availability SLAs in the quote
[11:18] Miguel Alvarez: what about streaming SDKs? we currently use websockets but nginx terminates and sometimes kills long-lived sockets
[11:28] Marco Reyes: websocket support is available for private/dedicated and we recommend TCP keepalive + application-level ping. for hosted we prefer SSE over HTTP/2 in our current gateway, but websockets are supported in private
[11:45] Sana Patel: you mentioned chunk size earlier - what's the recommended chunk size for low latency
[11:51] Marco Reyes: 64-256 tokens depending on your average token emission - smaller chunks reduce tail but increase overhead. Optimize's tuner can pick a sweet spot per workload
[12:10] Alice Chen: demo note: we also have a 'backpressure inspector' in the console that surfaces which prefixes got evicted and why, plus a timeline of requeue events - it was just that panel you saw
[12:25] Miguel Alvarez: nice, that would be helpful to troubleshoot production incidents
[12:31] Marco Reyes: next i'll show a POC plan outline - short runbook, benchmarks, and acceptance criteria. typical POC: 2 weeks, week 1 baseline capture + small-scale replay, week 2 full-scale replay with tweaks
[12:47] Jared Kim: acceptance criteria would be p95 latency <200ms and error rate <0.5% at your 500rps mix
[12:55] Marco Reyes: that'll be part of the runbook - we also collect quality metrics: hallucination/regression checks using your eval prompts
[13:08] Alice Chen: ok we've covered the tech; time for Q&A
[13:12] Sana Patel: one more on client retries: if we re-run a stream after a timeout how do you suggest deduping side effects downstream
[13:20] Marco Reyes: idempotency tokens are key. for streaming you can attach a session_id + request_id and we record the last-completed token index; you can either resume or re-run and the downstream can drop dupes
[13:34] Miguel Alvarez: will you help instrument that? we don't have a standard yet
[13:38] Marco Reyes: yes, SEs will provide example middleware; i'll add a snippet to the repo
[13:45] Jared Kim: ok what's the immediate next steps?
[13:50] Alice Chen: action items: we'll share pricing and perf spreadsheet, marco drafts runbook, and they'd share traffic sample. also schedule POC kickoff
[14:00] Miguel Alvarez: sounds good, can you include a quick checklist for nginx LB tweaks
[14:05] Marco Reyes: will do - we'll include recommended keepalive, idle timeout, and chunk heartbeat settings
[14:17] Jared Kim: one last question - what happens during model upgrades mid-session
[14:23] Marco Reyes: if model is incompatible the session's KV cache invalidates and we fail-safe to a small variant or we can drain sessions before upgrade in dedicated. we do a canary rollout with telemetry to watch quality regressions
[14:40] Alice Chen: great. thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with the documents and schedule. wrapping up

End of transcript
